brief.headline: AEGIS first launch: first-person view models in every crew seat, a 114-unit war across the whole landscape on three axes, and infantry that walk, aim and fall on an articulated rig.

items.text: AEGIS view models: enter any crew seat and you are holding something — rifle with iron sights, scoped M107, pintle .50 with a feeding belt, Apache canopy with glareshield MFDs, binoculars at the gun line. They sway with movement, kick with the unit's real recoil and muzzle-flash when it actually fires. Kept solid in both render modes deliberately: the weapon is the operator's hands, not part of the projection.

AEGIS theater-wide war: 114 units on three simultaneous axes — armour at the city, mech infantry in the hills, a recon screen on the flank — with fires in depth at the map edges whose 21/32 km reach covers every sector. Battle infantry now fight on foot on the articulated rig: walk on the advance, braced aim in contact, a fall about the feet when killed, rifle riding the hand throughout.

Playtested three full walk-in sessions end to end. Caught and fixed: battle stop() crashing on the new infantry rig fleets, view models eaten by the camera near plane, the holo wash rendering the weapon invisible, and table-scale civilians towering like giants over the metric battle from any eye-level camera (the crowd drops to metric scale whenever the camera is on the deck).

Found why the city disappeared on the owner's iPhone in photoreal mode. buildCity thinned its field to the 430-building budget and then pushed up to six signature towers in AFTER the cut, so it returned 434-436 — 12 of the first 15 sites over. index.html then asked GL to draw more instances than the buffer held. That is INVALID_OPERATION per the WebGL spec: Chrome tolerates it via robust buffer access and reports no error, which is why every desktop and headless test passed, while WebKit drops the whole draw call. Real mode made it total because the wireframe cages that survived in holo are faded to zero there. Fixed at the generator and guarded at the consumer; every skyline is unchanged.

AEGIS mobile HUD. The battle button was invisible: it used a crossed-swords glyph no font in the stack covers, so iOS drew tofu — a red square with an x, which reads as 'close'. Every control is now an SVG icon plus a word and nothing is under a 44px tap target (six of eight were about 20x22). Added COLLAPSE ALL as a floating pill plus per-panel folding: portrait canvas goes from 49.6% of the screen to 53.1%, 60.9% folded, 91.4% hidden. Also fixed the battle strip and every toast printing on top of each other inside the top bar, EXECUTE being unreachable in landscape, crew POV being an inescapable trap on a device with no ESC key, and no safe-area handling at all.

AEGIS roads. The streets were faked twice, independently, and the two fakes disagreed — a painted canvas with no data behind it, and a separate invented lane grid the cars drove on. So traffic ran on invisible lanes unrelated to the visible streets, through buildings. js/roadnet.js is now one directed graph that emits the ribbon mesh, the canvas overlay and the driveable lanes from the same nodes, laid out on the half-offsets of the building block step. Arterials and streets, signals, bridges, left-hand traffic. Zero buildings standing in a carriageway.

AEGIS locomotion. Pedestrians were one welded mesh and slid with a sine bob; all four wheels of every car were merged into one geometry, so a wheel could not physically turn. Five instanced parts now give a real walk cycle whose phase advances with DISTANCE TRAVELLED rather than the clock, and four instanced wheels per car roll off distance covered and steer off path curvature. Speeds were 2.5-6.6 m/s for a shopping crowd and 14-32 m/s for city traffic; both are honest now. The work surfaced that the merged person faced +X while the app rotates walkers to face +Z — the entire crowd had been walking sideways.
